# Video Generation Meets Agent Harness Agentic Video Generation, Agentic World Modeling and Recursive Self-Improvement

Liaoyuan Fan^(∗)  Yuhao Zheng^(∗)  Dongxing Mao^(∗) Hangyu Ran^(∗)
 Siyuan Hu^(∗)  Weijia Mao  Rui Zhao  
Weijia Wu  Guian Fang  Yanzhe Chen  Zeyu Zhu  Yuxin Jiang  Yiren Song
 Yuchao Gu  Junchao Yi  Qi Hu    
Dan Kong  Alex Jinpeng Wang  Kevin Qinghong Lin$`{}^{\text{\Letter}}`$
 Mike Zheng Shou$`{}^{\text{\Letter}}`$  Wei
Liu$`{}^{\text{\Letter}}`$  
Video Rebirth National University of Singapore Nanyang Technological
University Hong Kong University of Science and Technology University of

###### Abstract

Abstract: Video generation is evolving from end-to-end synthesis toward
agentic generation, in which planning, tool use, and feedback produce
coherent multi-shot videos with greater control. Meanwhile, video world
models provide action-conditioned observations and predicted futures and
can serve as interactive environments for agents. We study this
intersection through the agent harness: the executable runtime that
constructs an agent’s context, exposes tools, maintains state, routes
feedback, and enforces budgets around models such as video generators.
The report is organized around three directions. First, we study agentic
video generation, where harnesses coordinate script and shot planning,
asset management, shot production, and editing, and we discuss what the
evaluation of such systems must separate. Second, we examine agentic
world modeling, where harnesses mediate observation, control, execution,
and state, including designs in which a game engine or a program written
by a coding agent holds the world state while the video model renders
it, and where agents and world models test and improve one another.
Third, we examine recursive self-improvement (RSI) for video model
development: we separate revisions of a current output from updates to
harness state, generator parameters, and evaluators, and from changes to
the procedure that produces later updates, and we identify the channels
through which an improvement could re-enter development. Across these
directions, we analyze the agent capabilities that video imposes, from
audiovisual perception, long-horizon planning, and memory to interaction
through code and computer use, feedback-guided control, skill reuse, and
multi-agent organization. We conclude with open challenges, including
autonomous video production, lifelong memory, programmable hybrid
control, autonomous model development, provenance and cost accounting,
and evaluation that links video quality and task performance to
sustained improvement of models and harnesses.

Keywords: Video Generation, Agent, Harness Engineering, World Models,
Recursive Self-Improvement

## 1 Introduction

### 1.1 Motivation

Video generators produce increasingly realistic, controllable, and
temporally coherent clips \[kong2024hunyuanvideo\]. A generator alone,
however, does not organize the decisions needed to complete a video
task. A creative brief must become coherent shots; references must
persist across scenes; takes must be inspected; edits must preserve what
is correct \[huang2026vimax, vista2025\]. Interactive video must also
support continuing actions grounded in observations, not just a finished
clip \[gao2026lingbotworld2\]. These requirements motivate a transition
from video generation to agentic video generation: a goal-directed
process in which generated results inform subsequent decisions. An agent
can revise a plan, retrieve a reference, select a tool, or localize a
failure in response to actual outcomes \[li2026videogenagent\]. Agentic
video generation denotes a system-level perspective, not a new generator
architecture: the video model provides synthesis or predicted
transitions, while the agent makes consequential choices around those
capabilities. Video couples these choices over time. References affect
later shots \[chen2026cinecrew\], actions change subsequent
observations, and local repairs can disrupt temporal consistency
elsewhere. Plausible footage may still violate a narrative requirement
or fail to realize an intended action, so a quality score alone rarely
specifies what to do next \[liu2024videogenerationevaluation,
ding2026playworld\]. Effective control requires connecting observations
to localized decisions while maintaining project or interaction state
and accounting for generation cost.

The development from large language models (LLMs) to agents offers a
foundation for this control. Rather than only generating a response, an
LLM can operate within a cycle of reasoning, tool use, and observation,
as demonstrated by ReAct \[yao2023react\]. Planning and memory extend
this cycle to tasks requiring multiple decisions \[weng2023agents\].
Making these capabilities operational requires an agent harness: the
executable runtime around the model that constructs its context, exposes
tools, maintains state, routes feedback, and enforces permissions and
budgets \[weng2026harness, ning2026code\] (Section ). For video
generation, the harness is where a creative brief or an interactive goal
becomes executable operations on generators, editors, and world models.
The central question shifts from generating a good clip to reliably
completing a video task through feedback. Agentic video generation and
video world-model interaction are two concrete settings. A further
question is whether experience from these tasks can improve the system
that will perform future tasks.

![Refer to

Figure 2: Agent involvement across three directions of video generation.
Representative works branch from a shared video generation foundation
into agentic world modeling, agentic video generation, and development
toward recursive self-improvement (RSI). These directions connect video
models to sustained world interaction, coordinated production, and the
improvement of models and the agent harness. Vertical position reflects
increasing agent involvement, from No Agent through Agent Assistance and
Agent Guided Improvement to Self Improvement.

Feedback changes different objects at different timescales. Prompt
revision or take replacement targets the current artifact \[vista2025\];
retaining a skill targets subsequent tasks \[wei2026videoweaver\];
updating a dataset, critic, or generator targets later model versions
\[liu2025videoalign\]. These outcomes should not be conflated: effective
repair of a current video does not by itself establish improvement in
future capability. Beyond repairing individual outputs, context
engineering considers how instructions, retrieved evidence, memory, and
execution records are selected and organized for subsequent decisions
\[weng2026harness\]. Agentic Context Engineering (ACE), for example,
accumulates and revises a structured context from execution feedback
rather than updating model weights \[zhang2025ace\]. Such work shifts
attention from a current response toward reusable knowledge, while
leaving open whether the mechanisms that construct and update that
knowledge can themselves improve.

Recent work on automated research extends these ideas to model
development. The AI Scientist links idea generation, coding,
experiments, and reporting \[lu2024aiscientist\]; autoresearch runs a
bounded loop of training code modification, experimentation, and
validation-based acceptance \[karpathy2026autoresearch\]. These
workflows connect proposals to empirical feedback, but automating a
fixed experiment loop is not the same as improving the loop itself.
Research on self-improving agents, exemplified by the Darwin Gödel
Machine and Regularized Recursive Self-Improvement (RRSI), explores
changes to the agent’s own code or harness \[zhang2025dgm,
xia2026rrsi\]. Such work motivates examining the processes that generate
and validate subsequent improvements.

Recursive self-improvement (RSI) asks whether a system can improve the
procedures that produce further improvements \[chen2026surveyr04,
duan2026surveyn21\]. Video-specific targets include failure diagnosis,
data collection, supervision construction, update selection, and
candidate validation. Repeating a fixed collection-and-training pipeline
is iterative improvement. The recursive direction additionally allows
evidence to revise that pipeline, changing how a later round discovers
and addresses weaknesses. An agent harness provides an executable
surface for this direction. Its context construction, tool
orchestration, memory, testing workflow, and update-selection rules can
be inspected and, where authorized, revised \[weng2026harness\]. This
does not make every harness self-improving: a revision must be retained
and independently evaluated on later tasks or improvement rounds under
stated resource constraints \[xia2026rrsi\].

Existing video research supplies parts of this connection: feedback can
revise reusable production skills \[wei2026videoweaver\], uncertainty
can guide data acquisition for adaptation \[savov2025autoexplore\], and
validation can govern critic renewal for later training
\[yang2026dualipo\]. These are building blocks rather than evidence that
one system has completed the full RSI loop. Our survey therefore
connects three questions: how harnesses organize agentic video
generation, how they support video world-model interaction, and how they
may drive video-generation development toward RSI. The first two
establish task execution and sources of experience; the third examines
persistent capability and the procedures used to improve it. Figure
[2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1.1 Motivation ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Video Generation Meets Agent Harness Agentic Video Generation, Agentic World Modeling and Recursive Self-Improvement")
maps representative work from a shared video generation foundation into
the three directions corresponding to the questions below.

### 1.2 Contributions and Positioning

The survey addresses three questions about the influence of the agent
harness on video generation (Figure
[1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ Video Generation Meets Agent Harness Agentic Video Generation, Agentic World Modeling and Recursive Self-Improvement")),
each corresponding to one core chapter.

How does the agent harness enable agentic video generation? Agentic
Video Generation (Section ) studies how harnesses coordinate planning,
execution, tool use, memory, editing, and watermarking around shared
project state, and what the evaluation of such systems must separate. We
examine how feedback changes generation and editing decisions and how
those changes affect video quality, consistency, and efficiency.

How can the agent harness be integrated into video world models? Agentic
World Modeling (Section ) locates where a harness can intervene in
observation, control, execution, event organization, and state
management, and examines designs in which an engine holds the world
state while the video model renders it. We examine how these
interventions support sustained interaction, control fidelity, state
continuity, and agent-driven evaluation. The focus of this question is
how a harness enables reliable interaction with a video world model.

How can video generation systems move toward recursive self-improvement?
Toward RSI in Video Generation (Section ) examines how advances in video
generators and the agent harness can feed back into the process that
produces subsequent model improvements. We review foundation model
improvement, agent harness improvement, and evaluation, and identify the
channels through which gains in these components can strengthen failure
diagnosis, data curation, training, and validation in later development
rounds. The goal is to identify mechanisms and evidence needed for
recursively improving development processes that can support
next-generation video generation models.

These questions connect through feedback: agentic video generation and
world interaction can expose failures, while development can turn
selected evidence into changes deployed in later tasks. Section compares
the shared agent capabilities that support all three settings.

Differentiating Our Work from Existing Surveys

Existing surveys provide complementary accounts of video generation.
Work on spatiotemporal consistency examines generation models,
representations, training strategies, and evaluation, emphasizing the
mechanisms that maintain coherent video sequences
\[yin2025spatiotemporal\]. Post-training and alignment surveys organize
methods for adapting video generators to human intent, including
supervised fine-tuning, distillation, preference optimization, and
inference-time adaptation \[li2026videoposttraining\]. Evaluation
surveys examine perceptual quality, semantic fidelity, and alignment
with user instructions \[liu2024videogenerationevaluation\]. Together,
these accounts explain how video models are built, improved, and
assessed.

More directly related to our system perspective, agentic visual
generation surveys organize the conditioning, execution, and adaptation
decisions available to a controller across visual modalities
\[huang2026agenticvisual\], or study autonomous multimodal content
creation and the construction of stateful artifacts \[xu2026ags,
wang2026artifactcreation\]. Wu et al. place agentic generation and
world-modeling generation on a single capability ladder of visual
generation \[wu2026visualnewera\]. World model surveys characterize
predictive and simulation capabilities across domains, focus on action
conditioning, memory, and responsiveness in sustained interaction
\[chu2026agenticworldmodel, liu2026interactiveworldmodel\], or treat
world models as interactive proxies that supply feedback to continually
improving agents \[yang2026quovadis\]. Harness surveys analyze the
execution layer around text and coding agents \[ning2026code,
guo2026harnessdesign\]. Surveys of self-evolving agents and RSI examine
evolutionary targets, adaptation stages, and feedback loops across
general AI systems \[gao2025surveyr02, chen2026surveyr04,
wu2026rsisurvey\]. These perspectives share concepts such as feedback,
memory, and agent control, but none of them takes the harness around a
video generator as the unit of analysis across production, interaction,
and model development.

Table
[1.2](#S1.SS2 "1.2 Contributions and Positioning ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Video Generation Meets Agent Harness Agentic Video Generation, Agentic World Modeling and Recursive Self-Improvement")
compares related surveys and adjacent studies by scope, thematic
coverage (including RSI), and agent design. Our survey complements these
perspectives with a framework centered on video generation that covers
three settings in which a harness meets a video model: as a synthesizer
in production, as an interactive environment, and as the object of
development. The settings are linked through the harness: agents
organize generation and refinement, while video models provide
interactive experience that can inform agent decisions and further model
development. Where capability ladders treat agentic generation and world
modeling as successive stages of the generator \[wu2026visualnewera\],
we take the agent harness around the generator as the unit of analysis,
so that one framework covers production, interaction, and development.

Our contributions are threefold.

- •
  A harness-centered framework. We define a common agent–harness
  execution loop (Section ) and apply it to production, organized by
  workflow function (Section ), and to world-model interaction,
  organized by the interfaces through which a harness intervenes,
  including designs in which an engine or a program holds the world
  state (Section ).
- •
  An account of improvement. We separate revisions of the current output
  from updates to harness state, generator parameters, and evaluators,
  and from changes to the development procedure. We identify four
  channels through which an improvement could re-enter video
  development. No surveyed system yet revises the procedure that trains
  and validates the generator (Section ).
- •
  Evaluation requirements and open problems. We state how the agent
  harness supports active testing and reciprocal evaluation of agents
  and world models (Section ), what the evaluation of agentic production
  must separate (Section ), which capabilities video imposes on agents
  (Section ), and which challenges remain (Section ).
